titleEn: Namaḥ bows. Svāhā offers into the fire. Phaṭ strikes. The last word of a mantra is what it does.
meaningEn: The last word of a mantra is its action. Namaḥ is a bow — and it always tells you to whom: śivāya, to Śiva; gaṇapataye, to Gaṇapati; sarasvatyai, to Sarasvatī. Svāhā is the fire-word — the word that goes with the offering into the flame — 'well offered'; Agni carries it up. Phaṭ is a strike — a sharp, short sound that tradition hears as a cut and a guard, closing fierce mantras, often as hūṃ phaṭ. With these three, the shape of most seed-mantras can be read on sight: Oṃ, seed, name, and the action word.
meaningHi: मंत्र का आख़िरी शब्द उसका काम बताता है। नमः प्रणाम है — और हमेशा बताता है किसे: शिवाय, शिव को; गणपतये, गणपति को; सरस्वत्यै, सरस्वती को। स्वाहा आग का शब्द है — जो आहुति के साथ आग में जाता है — 'अच्छी तरह चढ़ाया'; अग्नि उसे ऊपर ले जाते हैं। फट् एक चोट है — छोटी, तेज़ आवाज़ जिसे परंपरा काटना और बचाना सुनती है, उग्र मंत्रों का अंत, अक्सर हूं फट्। ये तीन जान लें, तो ज़्यादातर बीज-मंत्रों का ढाँचा देखते ही पढ़ लेंगे: ॐ, बीज, नाम, और काम का शब्द।
sayItLike: na-mah (a soft breath after the h) · svaa-haa · p-hut — a p with a puff of air, never an f · hoom p-hut

words.glossEn: a bow — homage; always 'to' someone, named in the dative
words.grammar: the person bowed to takes the dative: śivāya, gaṇapataye, sarasvatyai, kālikāyai — that is why the name before namaḥ ends in -āya / -aye / -ai / -āyai

words.glossEn: the offering-word — the word that goes with the ghee into the fire
words.glossHi: आहुति का शब्द — जो घी के साथ आग में जाता है
words.root: su + āha — 'well said / well offered' (tradition's reading)
words.grammar: Vedic; every āhuti ends with it; closes Kṛṣṇa's mantra (…gopījanavallabhāya svāhā) and the Buddhist Tārā mantra (…ture svāhā)

words.glossEn: the striking-word — a sharp sound; tradition hears a cut, a guard
words.glossHi: चोट का शब्द — तेज़ आवाज़; परंपरा इसे काटना और बचाना सुनती है
words.grammar: tantric; ends with a stop, not a hum; the sound of a snap or a blow

words.glossEn: armour-seed, then strike — tradition's fierce close
words.glossHi: कवच, फिर चोट — रखवाली वाले मंत्रों का उग्र अंत
words.grammar: hūṃ is the kūrca / armour seed; phaṭ the blow — the pair closes Hanumān's longer mantra and many Devī mantras

source.text: Vedic usage for namaḥ and svāhā (Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda liturgy, everywhere an offering is made); tantric handbooks for phaṭ and hūṃ phaṭ (Śāradā-tilaka, 11th c.; Mantra-mahodadhi, 1588)
source.ref: namaḥ + dative: e.g. Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.8.1 (namaḥ śivāya); svāhā at every Vedic āhuti; phaṭ: Mantra-mahodadhi, Hanumat taraṅga (…hūṃ phaṭ)
source.note: Namaḥ and svāhā are Vedic and everywhere. Phaṭ belongs to the tantric layer; its 'cutting / guarding' sense is tradition's, and the meaning given for svāhā is tradition's reading, not a settled etymology.

significance.textSays: The Yajurveda's Śrī Rudram says 'namaḥ śivāya' — a bow, to Śiva, dative. Every Vedic offering ends 'svāhā'. The tantric handbooks close fierce mantras with 'hūṃ phaṭ'.
significance.traditionSays: Namaḥ is the humblest close and the commonest; svāhā belongs to the fire and to mantras that are offerings; phaṭ belongs to guarding and fierce mantras.
significance.weDoNotClaim: That phaṭ protects or that svāhā delivers anything. These are the grammar of what a mantra is doing; what it achieves is not promised.
